transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Hi. Yeah, nice to meet you too. Um, well, I guess I came in because... I just keep beating myself up lately. Like, I keep telling myself that I’m not really senior material at my job, and that I somehow fooled everyone into thinking I could handle way more than I actually can. 

Which, you know, I'm a computer systems analyst, and I got into it right out of high school. Back then, it was all about just knowing how to build a tower, you know? Me and my buddy used to set up these LAN networks in his garage just so we could play Doom. It was such a hassle with all the cables everywhere, and dial-up internet made that crazy screeching noise... man, I kind of miss that noise sometimes. You don't really hear anything like that anymore with fiber optics and Wi-Fi. It's all invisible now, which is cool, but it makes troubleshooting a totally different beast. 

But, um... what was I saying? Oh, right. Yeah, I just feel like a total fraud at work right now.
Did this start after something specific happened at work?

Yeah, actually. It was... I'd say about a month ago? They asked me to step up and cover the senior analyst duties because the guy who usually does it, Mark, he had to take some unexpected medical leave. 

Which, honestly, I felt really bad for the guy. He was having all these crazy lower back issues. You know how it is when you sit in those cheap corporate office chairs for ten hours a day, staring at screens. I kept telling him to get one of those ergonomic ones, or at least try a standing desk. I actually built my own standing desk at home out of some old heavy-duty crates and a solid core door I found at a salvage yard. Works like a charm, and it cost me basically nothing. My wife thought it was ugly, so I ended up staining the wood this dark cherry color, and now it actually looks pretty decent in the home office. 

But, uh, what was the question? Oh, right, work. Yeah, so Mark went on leave, and I had to take over his senior duties. And pretty much ever since then, for the last month or so, I've just had this really noticeable up-and-down pattern going on.
When you say your mood has been up and down, have there been times when you felt unusually energized or keyed up?

Yeah, definitely. Like, there was this one stretch where I just... I couldn't sit still at all after work. I'd log off, but my brain was still going a million miles an hour. I kept jumping back into server checks from home, and then I'd start on all these random home projects. Like, I decided I needed to fix the weather stripping on the back door, and then I was suddenly reorganizing the garage shelves... it just felt like everything had to be handled right then and there. 

Which is funny, because normally I hate doing the weather stripping. You have to scrape off all the old adhesive, and it gets under your fingernails. I tried using this citrus-based solvent I saw on YouTube, and it smelled great, kind of like those orange candies, you know? The ones wrapped in the clear plastic that look like little orange slices. My grandma used to keep a whole bowl of those on her coffee table, right next to these really creepy porcelain dolls she collected. I swear those dolls watched me whenever I tried to sneak a piece of candy. 

But yeah, I just had this crazy burst of energy where I couldn't stop doing little fixes around the house and checking work stuff.
During those high-energy stretches, were you needing less sleep than usual?

Yeah, actually, that was the weirdest part. For a while there, I was sleeping maybe three or four hours a night, tops. And I'd still wake up feeling totally ready to tackle the day, which is definitely not normal for me. Usually, if I don't get my solid seven hours, I'm practically a zombie by 2 PM. I have to drink this specific dark roast coffee just to keep my eyes open. 

I actually started buying my beans whole and grinding them myself. You get such a better flavor profile that way, you know? I got this burr grinder off Amazon—it's got like 40 different settings. It took me a week just to figure out the perfect grind size for my French press. You don't want it too fine, or it gets all sludgy at the bottom of the cup, but if it's too coarse, it just tastes like hot brown water. My wife hates the noise the grinder makes in the morning, though. She says it sounds like a garbage disposal eating rocks. 

But, um, anyway... yeah, three or four hours of sleep, and I was just totally fine. Ready to go.
During those high-energy periods, did you feel unusually confident or like you could do things better than other people?

Yeah, I guess you could say that. Before this recent low stretch I've been in, I had a few days where I felt almost... I don't know, too sure of myself? Like I had all the answers and everyone else was just dragging their feet. I'd find myself snapping at people over the dumbest little things. Like if someone took too long to reply to an email, or if a client asked the same question twice. 

Which, to be fair, is incredibly annoying. We have an FAQ document for a reason. I spent three days drafting that thing last year, formatting all the headers so they collapse and expand when you click them. It's really slick. I used this custom CSS script I found on a developer forum. The guy who wrote it lives in New Zealand, I think? We actually ended up messaging back and forth for a bit about mechanical keyboards. He built his own from scratch, soldering the switches and everything. I've been thinking about doing that, maybe getting those cherry blue switches because I like the clicky sound. My wife would probably murder me, though, especially after the coffee grinder thing. 

But yeah, I was definitely feeling pretty high and mighty for a few days there, just getting irritated when people couldn't keep up with me.
During those high-energy periods, were you talking more than usual or feeling like your words were coming out too fast?

I don't really think so. I mean, I haven't noticed myself talking any faster or more than I usually do. Most of my talking during the day is just on conference calls anyway, mostly over Teams. We actually just forced the whole department to migrate to Teams from Slack last month, and man, getting everyone's permissions transferred over was a total nightmare. Microsoft changes their admin center layout like every other week, I swear. 

I had to sit on hold with their enterprise support for an hour and a half just to get a licensing issue sorted out. The hold music was this weird jazz flute loop that just repeated every fifteen seconds. It drove me absolutely insane. I ended up muting my headset and just watching the call timer tick up on my second monitor. I have this ultrawide curved monitor now, which is amazing for having multiple server logs open side-by-side, but it takes up literally my entire desk. I had to buy a special heavy-duty monitor arm just to hold the weight of it, and even then it sort of sags if I bump the desk too hard. 

But um, what were you asking? Oh, right, talking fast. Yeah, no, I don't think my speech was any different than normal.
During those high-energy periods, did your behavior cause any problems at work or at home?

Well, I mean, I'm still making it to work every day. It hasn't gotten me fired or anything. But I have had to, like, double-check myself a lot more. Just making sure I'm not snapping at people or missing things. And I guess I've kind of pulled back from my friends and my wife lately, too. I just... I don't really trust my mood or my judgment right now, you know? 

Like, my buddy Dave invited me over to watch the game on Sunday. He just got this massive 85-inch OLED TV. It's ridiculous. The picture quality is insane, though. The true blacks on those OLED panels really make a huge difference, especially if you're watching a movie with a lot of dark scenes. You don't get that annoying blooming effect around bright objects like you do on regular LED screens. I was reading this whole breakdown on CNET about the pixel structure, and how LG is basically the only company actually manufacturing the panels, even for Sony and Vizio. It's crazy how consolidated the supply chain is for electronics right now. We had this huge issue at work last quarter trying to source replacement motherboards for our older servers because of some chip shortage in Taiwan. We ended up having to buy refurbished units off eBay just to keep the legacy systems running. 

But yeah, I told Dave I couldn't make it. I just didn't want to risk being weird or irritable around him, so I just stayed home.
During those high-energy stretches, were you getting a lot more done than usual?

Yeah, actually, I was getting a ton done. Like, way more than normal. I voluntarily took on all these extra monitoring reports that no one even asked me to do. And I was constantly messaging clients and coworkers with all these new ideas I had, just firing them off. It was almost like I was trying to prove I could run the whole department by myself, you know? 

Which honestly, sometimes I feel like I could. Half the people in my group don't even know how to run a basic SQL query. I had to show our new junior analyst how to do a simple JOIN the other day. He just graduated from some coding bootcamp, which I guess is the new thing now. Everyone wants to be a programmer in six weeks. I saw this ad on YouTube for one of those bootcamps that promised a six-figure salary right out of the gate. The ad had this guy sitting on a beach with his laptop, which is such a ridiculous cliché. Sand is terrible for electronics. I took my old ThinkPad to the beach once on vacation in Florida, and the fan sucked in so much grit it sounded like a blender for a month. We went to Siesta Key, supposedly the sand there is 99% quartz so it doesn't get hot on your feet. It's actually really cool, it feels like walking on powdered sugar. We stayed at this little Airbnb right off the main strip... 

Wait, sorry, what was the question? Oh, right, getting things done. Yeah, I was definitely cranking through the work and taking on extra stuff during those few days.
During those high-energy periods, did you do anything unusually impulsive or risky?

Well, I did spend a bunch of money. More than I probably should have, honestly. I just started buying all these certification courses online, thinking I was going to knock out like three new credentials in a month. And then I bought a bunch of vinyl records, and some new fishing gear. I don't even fish that much, but I got this crazy carbon fiber rod. The guy at the tackle shop was telling me how they bake the carbon at like 2,000 degrees to get the resin to set perfectly. It's the same process they use for Formula 1 car parts, which is wild when you think about it. The engineering that goes into F1 cars is just unbelievable. I watched this whole documentary on Netflix about the aerodynamics, and how they use wind tunnels to test the downforce. They have to run the wind tunnels 24/7 just to get enough data for one race weekend. It's such a massive waste of electricity, honestly, but the technology trickles down to regular cars eventually. Like those active spoilers on Porsches? Totally came from racing. My neighbor just bought a used Cayman, and he revs it in his driveway every morning at 6 AM. It wakes up my dog, and then the dog starts barking at the mailman... 

But anyway, yeah, I looked at my credit card bill a couple weeks later and just thought, man, what was I thinking? I definitely went a little overboard.
Did those high-energy periods last at least four days in a row?

Well, let's see... four days. I mean, it's hard to track exactly, but I don't think it was quite that long. Usually it just feels like a couple of days where I'm really wired, maybe two or three? It's kind of a blur when I'm in it. Time just moves differently, you know? Like when you're really in the zone working on a server migration and suddenly it's 3 AM and you forgot to eat dinner. That happened to me last month when we were moving everything to AWS. The latency issues were driving me crazy, trying to get the local database to sync with the cloud instances. Amazon's documentation is usually pretty good, but their IAM roles can be a nightmare to configure if you have a complex nested group structure. I ended up having to write a custom Python script just to map all the permissions correctly. Python is great for that kind of quick automation, though I still prefer C++ if I need something to run fast. My cousin is trying to learn Python right now, actually. He wants to build some kind of automated trading bot for crypto, which I told him is a terrible idea. The crypto market is so volatile, and the exchange APIs are constantly changing their rate limits. You can get your IP banned so fast if your code loops wrong. Plus, the tax implications of high-frequency crypto trading are a nightmare. My accountant was telling me last year... 

Wait, what did you ask? Four days? Yeah, no, I don't think it ever lasted four full days in a row. Just a couple days at a time, usually.
During this past month, have you had a period of at least two weeks when you felt down or depressed most of the day nearly every day?

Yeah, honestly, for the past few weeks, most days I've just had this heavy, low feeling. It's like I'm moving through work and home with the color turned down, you know? Everything just feels gray. Like that old black and white TV my grandparents used to have in their basement. It was one of those massive wooden console ones that weighed like two hundred pounds. You had to let the tubes warm up for five minutes before you could even see a picture. My grandfather refused to get rid of it because he said the sound quality was better than the new flat screens, which is actually kind of true because those old cabinets had real acoustic resonance. Now everyone just buys these cheap soundbars from Costco. I went to Costco last weekend to get paper towels and ended up spending two hundred dollars on random stuff. They put the bakery right by the entrance so you smell the bread and get hungry. It's a classic psychological trick, grocery stores do it all the time. They also put the milk all the way in the back so you have to walk past everything else to get it. I was reading this article about retail layout optimization, and they actually track where people's eyes look using the security cameras... 

Sorry, I'm doing it again. But yeah, to answer your question, it's been pretty consistently down and heavy like that for at least the last couple of weeks.
During these past couple of weeks, have you been having trouble concentrating?

Concentrating? I mean, I guess I haven't really noticed it being any worse than usual. I don't know, maybe? I just kind of sit at my desk and stare at the screen sometimes. But screens are so bad for your eyes anyway, especially the blue light. I bought these blue light blocking glasses online, but I'm pretty sure they're just regular plastic. The marketing for that stuff is so deceptive. It's like how they label food "all natural" when it's packed with high fructose corn syrup. Corn syrup is in literally everything now. They subsidize corn so much that it's cheaper to use that than real sugar. My uncle used to grow corn in Nebraska, actually. He had this massive combine harvester that cost more than my house. Those machines are incredibly complex, they use GPS to steer themselves so the rows are perfectly straight. It's crazy how much tech is in farming now. You'd think it was just tractors and dirt, but they're basically driving giant computers through the fields. 

So, yeah, I don't really know about the concentration thing. I haven't really paid attention to it.
During these past couple of weeks, have you lost interest or pleasure in things you usually enjoy?

Yeah, I guess so. I usually look forward to grilling on the weekend, you know, or maybe doing a little fishing down at the lake, or just putting on a record. But lately, I just leave the stuff sitting there and don't really care. I haven't fired up the grill in weeks. It's a Weber, one of the classic kettle ones. Charcoal, obviously. Propane is convenient, but you just don't get the same flavor. People say it doesn't matter, but if you use real hardwood lump charcoal instead of those briquettes, it makes a huge difference. The briquettes are full of binders and weird chemicals that make them burn evenly, but they leave this weird ashy taste on the meat. I was reading on a barbecue forum that some guys are making their own charcoal in these specialized kilns in their backyards. It sounds like a massive fire hazard, honestly. My neighbor almost burned his deck down last summer trying to deep fry a turkey. He didn't measure the oil displacement right and when he dropped the bird in, it just overflowed everywhere and caught the burner. The fire department had to come out and everything. They were actually pretty cool about it, let the kids look at the truck. Fire trucks are fascinating pieces of engineering, the water pressure they can generate is insane. They have these specialized PTO pumps that run off the main engine...

But anyway, yeah, I just haven't had the energy or interest to do any of my usual stuff lately. It's just sitting there.
Lately, have other people noticed that you seem slowed down in how you move or speak?

No, I don't think anyone's said anything like that. I mean, my wife usually tells me if I'm dragging, but she hasn't mentioned it. She's been super busy anyway, they just rolled out this new software system at her office and it's a total disaster. Typical enterprise software deployment, honestly. The vendors always promise it'll be seamless, but they never actually talk to the end users about their workflow. It's like building a house without asking the people moving in where they want the doors. I deal with this all the time at work. We had this one project manager who insisted on using Agile methodology for a hardware migration, which makes zero sense. You can't just iterate on physical servers once they're racked and cabled. Speaking of cables, I spent four hours last weekend trying to organize the rat's nest behind my TV. I bought all these velcro ties and cable sleeves, but it still looks terrible. The problem is all the different power bricks, they're too bulky to hide properly. I don't understand why everything can't just use standard USB-C power delivery by now. It would save so much e-waste. The amount of electronics we just throw away is staggering. There's this documentary about where all the old computers end up...

But no, to answer your question, nobody's mentioned me moving slow or talking slow or anything.
During these past couple of weeks, have you had thoughts that life isn’t worth living?

Life not worth living? I mean... I haven't made any kind of plan to hurt myself or anything like that. But I do catch myself thinking it might just be easier if I didn't wake up some morning. Just, you know, skip the whole routine. The routine is exhausting anyway. You get up, make the coffee, commute. The traffic on I-95 has been an absolute nightmare lately because they're doing that bridge repair. They've had two lanes closed for what feels like six months. The infrastructure in this country is just crumbling, it's unbelievable. I was reading this article about how they used to build bridges with these massive steel rivets, but now it's all high-strength bolts and tension cables. It's supposed to be better for handling seismic activity, but the maintenance costs are astronomical. They have to constantly inspect the tension on those cables using ultrasonic sensors. It's actually a pretty cool application of the technology. We use similar ultrasonic tech at work sometimes to check for micro-fractures in server racks when they get shipped, because the shipping companies just throw those boxes around like they're empty. You wouldn't believe the damage a forklift can do if the driver isn't paying attention. 

But yeah, I don't want to kill myself or anything. Just... sometimes I think it'd be easier to just sleep through it all.
During those wired, high-energy periods, did other people notice that you seemed different than your usual self?

Did people notice? Uh... I don't know, honestly. Nobody ever pulled me aside and said I was acting weird or anything. I mean, I get a lot done during those times, I'm just locked in. My typing speed goes way up, I know that much. I actually use a mechanical keyboard at work, one of those with the Cherry MX Blue switches. They're incredibly tactile, but they are so loud. It sounds like a machine gun going off when I get really going on a script. Some of my coworkers hate it. The whole open-plan office trend is just a disaster for productivity anyway. Whoever thought it was a good idea to put fifty systems analysts in one room with no walls clearly never had to write a line of code or troubleshoot a server. You can hear everything—people chewing, phone calls, the HVAC system humming. I had to invest in a pair of high-end noise-canceling headphones just to keep my sanity. The active noise cancellation on those things is basically magic, it uses these external microphones to create an exact inverse sound wave that cancels out the ambient noise. It's brilliant physics, really. 

But yeah, to your question, I don't think anyone really noticed me acting different, besides maybe typing a lot louder than usual.
Has this low mood been making it hard for you to function at work or at home?

Well, I'm still making it to work every day, so I guess I'm functioning. But I've definitely had to double-check my work a lot more lately. I just don't trust my own judgment right now, you know? It's like when you're writing a really complex SQL query and you forget a simple JOIN clause, and suddenly you're pulling a million rows instead of ten. That actually happened last Tuesday. I almost crashed the staging server because I was just staring at the screen and missed it. Staging servers are always under-provisioned anyway. Management never wants to spend the money to make the test environment match production, which completely defeats the purpose of having a test environment. If the hardware specs are different, how do you know the software is going to behave the same way under load? It's just basic logic. But try explaining that to the finance department when they're looking at the AWS bill. Cloud computing was supposed to save everyone money, but honestly, with all the data egress fees and instance costs, most companies would be better off just buying their own hardware and putting it in a colocation facility. At least then you own the metal. I used to work at this datacenter back in the early 2000s, and the cooling systems they had were incredible. Huge CRAC units blowing freezing air under the raised floor... 

But yeah, anyway. Work is a struggle, and honestly, I've kind of pulled back from my friends and family too. I just don't trust my mood, so it's easier to just stay away.
Do you feel all of this started mainly because of being asked to cover Mark’s senior duties at work?

Yeah, I'd say so. The noticeable up-and-down pattern really started about a month ago, right after they asked me to cover his senior analyst duties. Mark is the only guy who actually understood the legacy database integration we have. It's ridiculous, honestly. We still have this IBM AS/400 system running in a closet for our core inventory tracking. It's hardware from the nineties! I mean, it's built like a tank, sure, but the software is written in RPG, which is practically a dead language at this point. You can't even find developers for it anymore. If something breaks, management has to track down these retired guys and bring them in as consultants for like three hundred bucks an hour just to fix a batch processing error. I tried looking at the source code once and it's all fixed-format, column-based... it's an absolute nightmare to read if you're used to modern object-oriented languages. And the terminal emulators you have to use to access it, those old green screens? They give you such a headache if you stare at them too long. The refresh rate on the actual CRT monitors back in the day used to be terrible for your eyes, though I guess now we're just emulating it on flat screens, so it's really just the neon green text that's harsh. 

But yeah... wait, what was I saying? Right, Mark. Yeah, taking on his workload about a month ago is definitely when this whole rollercoaster started.
Do you feel your reaction to covering Mark’s duties has been much stronger than you would normally expect for that kind of work stress?

I mean, I don't know what a normal reaction is supposed to look like anymore. Is it stronger than normal? Maybe? But the stress is just... it's constant. And it's not just the extra work, it's the expectation that I should just know how to do it. Mark had been here for fifteen years. You don't just absorb fifteen years of institutional knowledge overnight. It's like trying to reverse-engineer a compiled executable without the source code. You can look at the assembly language all day, but unless you know the original logic the programmer was using, you're just guessing. I actually spent a weekend once trying to decompile this old shareware game from the nineties just to see how they handled the sprite rendering. Back then, they had to use all these crazy bit-shifting tricks because the processors were so slow. You couldn't just throw raw compute power at a problem like you can today. Now, developers don't even care about optimization. They just write bloated code and expect the hardware to compensate. That's why web browsers use so much RAM now. You open three tabs and suddenly Chrome is eating up four gigabytes of memory. It's completely inefficient. 

But, uh, as for the stress... I don't know if my reaction is stronger than it should be. It just feels like a lot to handle all at once.
Over the past month, have you been worrying a lot more than usual?

I guess I've been worrying, yeah. But who wouldn't be worrying? It's just... there's so much to keep track of now. And worrying is practically part of the job description in IT. If you're not worrying about a security vulnerability, you're not doing your job. Like that Log4j exploit that happened a while back? That was a nightmare. Every single company on the planet was scrambling to patch their Java applications. And the crazy thing is, it was just this tiny, open-source logging library that some guy was maintaining in his spare time for free, and it was running on millions of enterprise servers. It really makes you think about how fragile the whole software ecosystem is. We build these massive, mission-critical systems on top of free code written by hobbyists. It's like building a skyscraper on a foundation of toothpicks. Open-source is great for innovation, obviously, but the funding model is completely broken. Corporations make billions off of Linux and Apache, but they barely donate anything back to the maintainers. It's just exploitation, really. 

But anyway, worrying... I don't know if it's more than usual. It just feels like there's always something hanging over my head right now.

patient.answer:
Hi. Yeah, nice to meet you too. Um, well, I guess I came in because... I just keep beating myself up lately. Like, I keep telling myself that I’m not really senior material at my job, and that I somehow fooled everyone into thinking I could handle way more than I actually can. 

Which, you know, I'm a computer systems analyst, and I got into it right out of high school. Back then, it was all about just knowing how to build a tower, you know? Me and my buddy used to set up these LAN networks in his garage just so we could play Doom. It was such a hassle with all the cables everywhere, and dial-up internet made that crazy screeching noise... man, I kind of miss that noise sometimes. You don't really hear anything like that anymore with fiber optics and Wi-Fi. It's all invisible now, which is cool, but it makes troubleshooting a totally different beast. 

But, um... what was I saying? Oh, right. Yeah, I just feel like a total fraud at work right now.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the distress is tied specifically to a recent identifiable work stressor, which would help distinguish adjustment disorder or a work-related problem from generalized anxiety, depression, or avoidant personality traits.
doctor.question: Did this start after something specific happened at work?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: The noticeable up-and-down pattern really started about a month ago, after I was asked to cover the senior analyst duties.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the onset of the symptoms and if they started after a specific event at work, which corresponds to the Duration item where the patient mentions the pattern started about a month ago after being asked to cover senior analyst duties.

patient.answer:
Yeah, actually. It was... I'd say about a month ago? They asked me to step up and cover the senior analyst duties because the guy who usually does it, Mark, he had to take some unexpected medical leave. 

Which, honestly, I felt really bad for the guy. He was having all these crazy lower back issues. You know how it is when you sit in those cheap corporate office chairs for ten hours a day, staring at screens. I kept telling him to get one of those ergonomic ones, or at least try a standing desk. I actually built my own standing desk at home out of some old heavy-duty crates and a solid core door I found at a salvage yard. Works like a charm, and it cost me basically nothing. My wife thought it was ugly, so I ended up staining the wood this dark cherry color, and now it actually looks pretty decent in the home office. 

But, uh, what was the question? Oh, right, work. Yeah, so Mark went on leave, and I had to take over his senior duties. And pretty much ever since then, for the last month or so, I've just had this really noticeable up-and-down pattern going on.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the mood change is episodic with discrete periods of elevated or unusually energized mood, which would clarify what the patient means by an up-and-down pattern and help distinguish stress-related anxiety/depression from a mood episode.
doctor.question: When you say your mood has been up and down, have there been times when you felt unusually energized or keyed up?

target_item.name: Increased_Activity
target_item.manifestation: During that same stretch I couldn’t sit still after work and kept jumping into server checks, home projects, and little fixes around the house like everything had to be handled right then.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about times when the patient felt 'unusually energized or keyed up', which maps to increased goal-directed activity or energy.

patient.answer:
Yeah, definitely. Like, there was this one stretch where I just... I couldn't sit still at all after work. I'd log off, but my brain was still going a million miles an hour. I kept jumping back into server checks from home, and then I'd start on all these random home projects. Like, I decided I needed to fix the weather stripping on the back door, and then I was suddenly reorganizing the garage shelves... it just felt like everything had to be handled right then and there. 

Which is funny, because normally I hate doing the weather stripping. You have to scrape off all the old adhesive, and it gets under your fingernails. I tried using this citrus-based solvent I saw on YouTube, and it smelled great, kind of like those orange candies, you know? The ones wrapped in the clear plastic that look like little orange slices. My grandma used to keep a whole bowl of those on her coffee table, right next to these really creepy porcelain dolls she collected. I swear those dolls watched me whenever I tried to sneak a piece of candy. 

But yeah, I just had this crazy burst of energy where I couldn't stop doing little fixes around the house and checking work stuff.

inference.note: Added F31.81 due to a month-long onset after increased work stress with distinct periods of elevated energy, inability to sit still, racing thoughts, and increased goal-directed activity. doctor.intent: Determine whether the elevated-energy periods involve decreased need for sleep, which best distinguishes bipolar spectrum hypomania from anxiety, adjustment disorder, or unipolar depression.

target_item.name: Decreased_Sleep
target_item.manifestation: For a while I was sleeping maybe three or four hours and still getting up feeling ready to tackle the day, which is not normal for me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking if I needed less sleep than usual during my high-energy stretches, which maps to the Decreased Sleep symptom.

patient.answer:
Yeah, actually, that was the weirdest part. For a while there, I was sleeping maybe three or four hours a night, tops. And I'd still wake up feeling totally ready to tackle the day, which is definitely not normal for me. Usually, if I don't get my solid seven hours, I'm practically a zombie by 2 PM. I have to drink this specific dark roast coffee just to keep my eyes open. 

I actually started buying my beans whole and grinding them myself. You get such a better flavor profile that way, you know? I got this burr grinder off Amazon—it's got like 40 different settings. It took me a week just to figure out the perfect grind size for my French press. You don't want it too fine, or it gets all sludgy at the bottom of the cup, but if it's too coarse, it just tastes like hot brown water. My wife hates the noise the grinder makes in the morning, though. She says it sounds like a garbage disposal eating rocks. 

But, um, anyway... yeah, three or four hours of sleep, and I was just totally fine. Ready to go.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the energized periods included abnormally elevated self-esteem or grandiosity, which would help distinguish bipolar II hypomania from anxiety, adjustment disorder, or unipolar depression.

patient.answer:
Yeah, I guess you could say that. Before this recent low stretch I've been in, I had a few days where I felt almost... I don't know, too sure of myself? Like I had all the answers and everyone else was just dragging their feet. I'd find myself snapping at people over the dumbest little things. Like if someone took too long to reply to an email, or if a client asked the same question twice. 

Which, to be fair, is incredibly annoying. We have an FAQ document for a reason. I spent three days drafting that thing last year, formatting all the headers so they collapse and expand when you click them. It's really slick. I used this custom CSS script I found on a developer forum. The guy who wrote it lives in New Zealand, I think? We actually ended up messaging back and forth for a bit about mechanical keyboards. He built his own from scratch, soldering the switches and everything. I've been thinking about doing that, maybe getting those cherry blue switches because I like the clicky sound. My wife would probably murder me, though, especially after the coffee grinder thing. 

But yeah, I was definitely feeling pretty high and mighty for a few days there, just getting irritated when people couldn't keep up with me.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the elevated-energy periods included increased talkativeness/pressured speech, which would help distinguish hypomania (bipolar II) from anxiety, adjustment disorder, or unipolar depression.

We actually just forced the whole department to migrate to Teams from Slack last month, and man, getting everyone's permissions transferred over was a total nightmare. Microsoft changes their admin center layout like every other week, I swear. 

I had to sit on hold with their enterprise support for an hour and a half just to get a licensing issue sorted out. The hold music was this weird jazz flute loop that just repeated every fifteen seconds. It drove me absolutely insane. I ended up muting my headset and just watching the call timer tick up on my second monitor. I have this ultrawide curved monitor now, which is amazing for having multiple server logs open side-by-side, but it takes up literally my entire desk. I had to buy a special heavy-duty monitor arm just to hold the weight of it, and even then it sort of sags if I bump the desk too hard. 

But um, what were you asking? Oh, right, talking fast. Yeah, no, I don't think my speech was any different than normal.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the elevated-energy periods caused observable functional impairment or consequences severe enough to support hypomania rather than anxiety or adjustment-related distress.

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’m still making it to work, but I’ve had to double-check myself more and I’ve pulled back from friends and family because I don’t trust my mood or my judgment lately.

Just making sure I'm not snapping at people or missing things. And I guess I've kind of pulled back from my friends and my wife lately, too. I just... I don't really trust my mood or my judgment right now, you know? 

Like, my buddy Dave invited me over to watch the game on Sunday. He just got this massive 85-inch OLED TV. It's ridiculous. The picture quality is insane, though. The true blacks on those OLED panels really make a huge difference, especially if you're watching a movie with a lot of dark scenes. You don't get that annoying blooming effect around bright objects like you do on regular LED screens. I was reading this whole breakdown on CNET about the pixel structure, and how LG is basically the only company actually manufacturing the panels, even for Sony and Vizio. It's crazy how consolidated the supply chain is for electronics right now. We had this huge issue at work last quarter trying to source replacement motherboards for our older servers because of some chip shortage in Taiwan. We ended up having to buy refurbished units off eBay just to keep the legacy systems running. 

But yeah, I told Dave I couldn't make it. I just didn't want to risk being weird or irritable around him, so I just stayed home.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the elevated-energy periods included abnormally increased goal-directed activity, which helps distinguish hypomania from anxiety or adjustment-related distress.

target_item.name: Increased_Goal_Activity
target_item.manifestation: I took on extra monitoring reports and started messaging clients and coworkers with ideas before anyone asked, like I was trying to prove I could run the whole thing myself.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question about 'getting a lot more done than usual' directly asks about an increase in goal-directed activity, which matches this symptom.

patient.answer:
Yeah, actually, I was getting a ton done. Like, way more than normal. I voluntarily took on all these extra monitoring reports that no one even asked me to do. And I was constantly messaging clients and coworkers with all these new ideas I had, just firing them off. It was almost like I was trying to prove I could run the whole department by myself, you know? 

Which honestly, sometimes I feel like I could. Half the people in my group don't even know how to run a basic SQL query. I had to show our new junior analyst how to do a simple JOIN the other day. He just graduated from some coding bootcamp, which I guess is the new thing now. Everyone wants to be a programmer in six weeks. I saw this ad on YouTube for one of those bootcamps that promised a six-figure salary right out of the gate. The ad had this guy sitting on a beach with his laptop, which is such a ridiculous cliché. Sand is terrible for electronics. I took my old ThinkPad to the beach once on vacation in Florida, and the fan sucked in so much grit it sounded like a blender for a month. We went to Siesta Key, supposedly the sand there is 99% quartz so it doesn't get hot on your feet. It's actually really cool, it feels like walking on powdered sugar. We stayed at this little Airbnb right off the main strip... 

Wait, sorry, what was the question? Oh, right, getting things done. Yeah, I was definitely cranking through the work and taking on extra stuff during those few days.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the elevated-energy episodes included impulsive or risky behavior, which would help distinguish bipolar II hypomania from stress-related mood changes or unipolar depression.
doctor.question: During those high-energy periods, did you do anything unusually impulsive or risky?

target_item.name: Painful_Consequence_Behavior
target_item.manifestation: I spent more than I should have on certification courses, records, and fishing gear all in a short run, and later I looked at the card bill wondering what I was thinking.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about impulsive or risky behavior during high-energy periods, which matches the symptom of excessive involvement in activities with high potential for painful consequences.

patient.answer:
Well, I did spend a bunch of money. More than I probably should have, honestly. I just started buying all these certification courses online, thinking I was going to knock out like three new credentials in a month. And then I bought a bunch of vinyl records, and some new fishing gear. I don't even fish that much, but I got this crazy carbon fiber rod. The guy at the tackle shop was telling me how they bake the carbon at like 2,000 degrees to get the resin to set perfectly. It's the same process they use for Formula 1 car parts, which is wild when you think about it. The engineering that goes into F1 cars is just unbelievable. I watched this whole documentary on Netflix about the aerodynamics, and how they use wind tunnels to test the downforce. They have to run the wind tunnels 24/7 just to get enough data for one race weekend. It's such a massive waste of electricity, honestly, but the technology trickles down to regular cars eventually. Like those active spoilers on Porsches? Totally came from racing. My neighbor just bought a used Cayman, and he revs it in his driveway every morning at 6 AM. It wakes up my dog, and then the dog starts barking at the mailman... 

But anyway, yeah, I looked at my credit card bill a couple weeks later and just thought, man, what was I thinking? I definitely went a little overboard.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the elevated periods lasted at least 4 days, which would distinguish hypomania in bipolar II disorder from other causes of mood symptoms.
doctor.question: Did those high-energy periods last at least four days in a row?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the specific duration (at least 4 days) of the high-energy/hypomanic periods. While the profile mentions they lasted 'several days' (under Elevated_Irritable_Mood), there is no specific key for the duration of the hypomanic episodes.

patient.answer:
Well, let's see... four days. I mean, it's hard to track exactly, but I don't think it was quite that long. Usually it just feels like a couple of days where I'm really wired, maybe two or three? It's kind of a blur when I'm in it. Time just moves differently, you know? Like when you're really in the zone working on a server migration and suddenly it's 3 AM and you forgot to eat dinner. That happened to me last month when we were moving everything to AWS. The latency issues were driving me crazy, trying to get the local database to sync with the cloud instances. Amazon's documentation is usually pretty good, but their IAM roles can be a nightmare to configure if you have a complex nested group structure. I ended up having to write a custom Python script just to map all the permissions correctly. Python is great for that kind of quick automation, though I still prefer C++ if I need something to run fast. My cousin is trying to learn Python right now, actually. He wants to build some kind of automated trading bot for crypto, which I told him is a terrible idea. The crypto market is so volatile, and the exchange APIs are constantly changing their rate limits. You can get your IP banned so fast if your code loops wrong. Plus, the tax implications of high-frequency crypto trading are a nightmare. My accountant was telling me last year... 

Wait, what did you ask? Four days? Yeah, no, I don't think it ever lasted four full days in a row. Just a couple days at a time, usually.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has had a sustained major depressive episode, which would help distinguish bipolar II disorder from brief stress-related mood changes or generalized anxiety.
doctor.question: During this past month, have you had a period of at least two weeks when you felt down or depressed most of the day nearly every day?

target_item.name: Depressed_Mood
target_item.manifestation: Most days lately I’ve had this heavy, low feeling, like I’m just moving through work and home with the color turned down.

Yeah, honestly, for the past few weeks, most days I've just had this heavy, low feeling. It's like I'm moving through work and home with the color turned down, you know? Everything just feels gray. Like that old black and white TV my grandparents used to have in their basement. It was one of those massive wooden console ones that weighed like two hundred pounds. You had to let the tubes warm up for five minutes before you could even see a picture. My grandfather refused to get rid of it because he said the sound quality was better than the new flat screens, which is actually kind of true because those old cabinets had real acoustic resonance. Now everyone just buys these cheap soundbars from Costco. I went to Costco last weekend to get paper towels and ended up spending two hundred dollars on random stuff. They put the bakery right by the entrance so you smell the bread and get hungry. It's a classic psychological trick, grocery stores do it all the time. They also put the milk all the way in the back so you have to walk past everything else to get it. I was reading this article about retail layout optimization, and they actually track where people's eyes look using the security cameras... 

Sorry, I'm doing it again. But yeah, to answer your question, it's been pretty consistently down and heavy like that for at least the last couple of weeks.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the current depressive episode includes impaired concentration, which helps distinguish major depressive episode/bipolar spectrum depression from generalized anxiety or adjustment disorder.

Concentrating? I mean, I guess I haven't really noticed it being any worse than usual. I don't know, maybe? I just kind of sit at my desk and stare at the screen sometimes. But screens are so bad for your eyes anyway, especially the blue light. I bought these blue light blocking glasses online, but I'm pretty sure they're just regular plastic. The marketing for that stuff is so deceptive. It's like how they label food "all natural" when it's packed with high fructose corn syrup. Corn syrup is in literally everything now. They subsidize corn so much that it's cheaper to use that than real sugar. My uncle used to grow corn in Nebraska, actually. He had this massive combine harvester that cost more than my house. Those machines are incredibly complex, they use GPS to steer themselves so the rows are perfectly straight. It's crazy how much tech is in farming now. You'd think it was just tractors and dirt, but they're basically driving giant computers through the fields. 

So, yeah, I don't really know about the concentration thing. I haven't really paid attention to it.

Yeah, I guess so. I usually look forward to grilling on the weekend, you know, or maybe doing a little fishing down at the lake, or just putting on a record. But lately, I just leave the stuff sitting there and don't really care. I haven't fired up the grill in weeks. It's a Weber, one of the classic kettle ones. Charcoal, obviously. Propane is convenient, but you just don't get the same flavor. People say it doesn't matter, but if you use real hardwood lump charcoal instead of those briquettes, it makes a huge difference. The briquettes are full of binders and weird chemicals that make them burn evenly, but they leave this weird ashy taste on the meat. I was reading on a barbecue forum that some guys are making their own charcoal in these specialized kilns in their backyards. It sounds like a massive fire hazard, honestly. My neighbor almost burned his deck down last summer trying to deep fry a turkey. He didn't measure the oil displacement right and when he dropped the bird in, it just overflowed everywhere and caught the burner. The fire department had to come out and everything. They were actually pretty cool about it, let the kids look at the truck. Fire trucks are fascinating pieces of engineering, the water pressure they can generate is insane. They have these specialized PTO pumps that run off the main engine...

But anyway, yeah, I just haven't had the energy or interest to do any of my usual stuff lately. It's just sitting there.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the current depressive symptoms are causing clinically significant psychomotor slowing, which would support a major depressive episode over adjustment disorder and help clarify severity.

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about psychomotor retardation (being slowed down in movement or speech), which is not listed in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
No, I don't think anyone's said anything like that. I mean, my wife usually tells me if I'm dragging, but she hasn't mentioned it. She's been super busy anyway, they just rolled out this new software system at her office and it's a total disaster. Typical enterprise software deployment, honestly. The vendors always promise it'll be seamless, but they never actually talk to the end users about their workflow. It's like building a house without asking the people moving in where they want the doors. I deal with this all the time at work. We had this one project manager who insisted on using Agile methodology for a hardware migration, which makes zero sense. You can't just iterate on physical servers once they're racked and cabled. Speaking of cables, I spent four hours last weekend trying to organize the rat's nest behind my TV. I bought all these velcro ties and cable sleeves, but it still looks terrible. The problem is all the different power bricks, they're too bulky to hide properly. I don't understand why everything can't just use standard USB-C power delivery by now. It would save so much e-waste. The amount of electronics we just throw away is staggering. There's this documentary about where all the old computers end up...

But no, to answer your question, nobody's mentioned me moving slow or talking slow or anything.

doctor.intent: Assess suicidality to distinguish a major depressive episode severity and immediate risk from adjustment disorder or anxiety
doctor.question: During these past couple of weeks, have you had thoughts that life isn’t worth living?

target_item.name: Death_Suicide
target_item.manifestation: I haven’t made any plan to hurt myself, but I do catch myself thinking it might be easier if I just didn’t wake up some morning.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about thoughts of life not being worth living, which directly corresponds to the Death_Suicide symptom profile concerning suicidal ideation or thoughts of death.

patient.answer:
Life not worth living? I mean... I haven't made any kind of plan to hurt myself or anything like that. But I do catch myself thinking it might just be easier if I didn't wake up some morning. Just, you know, skip the whole routine. The routine is exhausting anyway. You get up, make the coffee, commute. The traffic on I-95 has been an absolute nightmare lately because they're doing that bridge repair. They've had two lanes closed for what feels like six months. The infrastructure in this country is just crumbling, it's unbelievable. I was reading this article about how they used to build bridges with these massive steel rivets, but now it's all high-strength bolts and tension cables. It's supposed to be better for handling seismic activity, but the maintenance costs are astronomical. They have to constantly inspect the tension on those cables using ultrasonic sensors. It's actually a pretty cool application of the technology. We use similar ultrasonic tech at work sometimes to check for micro-fractures in server racks when they get shipped, because the shipping companies just throw those boxes around like they're empty. You wouldn't believe the damage a forklift can do if the driver isn't paying attention. 

But yeah, I don't want to kill myself or anything. Just... sometimes I think it'd be easier to just sleep through it all.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the elevated periods were observable by others as a clear change in functioning, which would help distinguish hypomanic symptoms from stress-related mood shifts or depression/anxiety.
doctor.question: During those wired, high-energy periods, did other people notice that you seemed different than your usual self?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the change in mood and behavior was observable by others (a diagnostic criterion for hypomanic/manic episodes), which does not directly map to a specific symptom in the provided profile.

patient.answer:
Did people notice? Uh... I don't know, honestly. Nobody ever pulled me aside and said I was acting weird or anything. I mean, I get a lot done during those times, I'm just locked in. My typing speed goes way up, I know that much. I actually use a mechanical keyboard at work, one of those with the Cherry MX Blue switches. They're incredibly tactile, but they are so loud. It sounds like a machine gun going off when I get really going on a script. Some of my coworkers hate it. The whole open-plan office trend is just a disaster for productivity anyway. Whoever thought it was a good idea to put fifty systems analysts in one room with no walls clearly never had to write a line of code or troubleshoot a server. You can hear everything—people chewing, phone calls, the HVAC system humming. I had to invest in a pair of high-end noise-canceling headphones just to keep my sanity. The active noise cancellation on those things is basically magic, it uses these external microphones to create an exact inverse sound wave that cancels out the ambient noise. It's brilliant physics, really. 

But yeah, to your question, I don't think anyone really noticed me acting different, besides maybe typing a lot louder than usual.

doctor.intent: Assess whether the depressive episode is causing clinically significant impairment, to distinguish major depressive disorder from adjustment disorder with mixed anxiety and depressed mood.
doctor.question: Has this low mood been making it hard for you to function at work or at home?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’m still making it to work, but I’ve had to double-check myself more and I’ve pulled back from friends and family because I don’t trust my mood or my judgment lately.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking how the mood symptoms have impacted my ability to function at work and home, which directly maps to functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Well, I'm still making it to work every day, so I guess I'm functioning. But I've definitely had to double-check my work a lot more lately. I just don't trust my own judgment right now, you know? It's like when you're writing a really complex SQL query and you forget a simple JOIN clause, and suddenly you're pulling a million rows instead of ten. That actually happened last Tuesday. I almost crashed the staging server because I was just staring at the screen and missed it. Staging servers are always under-provisioned anyway. Management never wants to spend the money to make the test environment match production, which completely defeats the purpose of having a test environment. If the hardware specs are different, how do you know the software is going to behave the same way under load? It's just basic logic. But try explaining that to the finance department when they're looking at the AWS bill. Cloud computing was supposed to save everyone money, but honestly, with all the data egress fees and instance costs, most companies would be better off just buying their own hardware and putting it in a colocation facility. At least then you own the metal. I used to work at this datacenter back in the early 2000s, and the cooling systems they had were incredible. Huge CRAC units blowing freezing air under the raised floor... 

But yeah, anyway. Work is a struggle, and honestly, I've kind of pulled back from my friends and family too. I just don't trust my mood, so it's easier to just stay away.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the recent depressive and high-energy symptoms are tied to an identifiable stressor, which would help distinguish an adjustment disorder from a primary mood disorder.
doctor.question: Do you feel all of this started mainly because of being asked to cover Mark’s senior duties at work?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: The noticeable up-and-down pattern really started about a month ago, after I was asked to cover the senior analyst duties.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about when and why the symptoms started, which perfectly matches the 'duration' item discussing the onset of the up-and-down pattern after being asked to cover senior analyst duties.

patient.answer:
Yeah, I'd say so. The noticeable up-and-down pattern really started about a month ago, right after they asked me to cover his senior analyst duties. Mark is the only guy who actually understood the legacy database integration we have. It's ridiculous, honestly. We still have this IBM AS/400 system running in a closet for our core inventory tracking. It's hardware from the nineties! I mean, it's built like a tank, sure, but the software is written in RPG, which is practically a dead language at this point. You can't even find developers for it anymore. If something breaks, management has to track down these retired guys and bring them in as consultants for like three hundred bucks an hour just to fix a batch processing error. I tried looking at the source code once and it's all fixed-format, column-based... it's an absolute nightmare to read if you're used to modern object-oriented languages. And the terminal emulators you have to use to access it, those old green screens? They give you such a headache if you stare at them too long. The refresh rate on the actual CRT monitors back in the day used to be terrible for your eyes, though I guess now we're just emulating it on flat screens, so it's really just the neon green text that's harsh. 

But yeah... wait, what was I saying? Right, Mark. Yeah, taking on his workload about a month ago is definitely when this whole rollercoaster started.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the depressive and mood symptoms are out of proportion to the work stressor, helping distinguish adjustment disorder with mixed anxiety and depressed mood from a primary mood disorder.
doctor.question: Do you feel your reaction to covering Mark’s duties has been much stronger than you would normally expect for that kind of work stress?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if my reaction to the stressor is disproportionate, which relates to ruling out Adjustment Disorder, but this does not map to any specific symptom in my profile.

patient.answer:
I mean, I don't know what a normal reaction is supposed to look like anymore. Is it stronger than normal? Maybe? But the stress is just... it's constant. And it's not just the extra work, it's the expectation that I should just know how to do it. Mark had been here for fifteen years. You don't just absorb fifteen years of institutional knowledge overnight. It's like trying to reverse-engineer a compiled executable without the source code. You can look at the assembly language all day, but unless you know the original logic the programmer was using, you're just guessing. I actually spent a weekend once trying to decompile this old shareware game from the nineties just to see how they handled the sprite rendering. Back then, they had to use all these crazy bit-shifting tricks because the processors were so slow. You couldn't just throw raw compute power at a problem like you can today. Now, developers don't even care about optimization. They just write bloated code and expect the hardware to compensate. That's why web browsers use so much RAM now. You open three tabs and suddenly Chrome is eating up four gigabytes of memory. It's completely inefficient. 

But, uh, as for the stress... I don't know if my reaction is stronger than it should be. It just feels like a lot to handle all at once.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the depressive symptoms are accompanied by significant anxiety and worry, which would support adjustment disorder with mixed anxiety and depressed mood or generalized anxiety disorder over a primary depressive or bipolar-spectrum diagnosis.
doctor.question: Over the past month, have you been worrying a lot more than usual?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about excessive worry or anxiety, which is not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
I guess I've been worrying, yeah. But who wouldn't be worrying? It's just... there's so much to keep track of now. And worrying is practically part of the job description in IT. If you're not worrying about a security vulnerability, you're not doing your job. Like that Log4j exploit that happened a while back? That was a nightmare. Every single company on the planet was scrambling to patch their Java applications. And the crazy thing is, it was just this tiny, open-source logging library that some guy was maintaining in his spare time for free, and it was running on millions of enterprise servers. It really makes you think about how fragile the whole software ecosystem is. We build these massive, mission-critical systems on top of free code written by hobbyists. It's like building a skyscraper on a foundation of toothpicks. Open-source is great for innovation, obviously, but the funding model is completely broken. Corporations make billions off of Linux and Apache, but they barely donate anything back to the maintainers. It's just exploitation, really. 

But anyway, worrying... I don't know if it's more than usual. It just feels like there's always something hanging over my head right now.

opening_question.intent: Learn the patient's main reason for seeking psychiatric care today
opening_question.question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: Symptoms began within about 1 month of a clear work-related stressor (covering senior duties after a colleague’s medical leave) and include mixed anxiety/depressive features: persistent low mood for at least 2 weeks, reduced interest, passive death wishes, self-doubt, increased worry, and functional strain/social withdrawal. Although there were brief high-energy periods with decreased sleep, increased productivity, irritability, spending, and inflated confidence, these episodes did not last at least 4 days and were not clearly observable by others, so criteria for hypomania/Bipolar II were not met. Major depressive disorder is less fitting because the presentation is closely tied to an identifiable psychosocial stressor and does not clearly establish a full major depressive episode. Generalized anxiety disorder is less fitting because excessive worry was not clearly pervasive for 6 months and the picture is predominantly stressor-linked with concurrent depressive symptoms.
